A hash table is a way of organizing information so that a lookup can often jump almost directly to the answer instead of searching through everything. The central idea is to turn the key you are looking for into a number, and then use that number as an address inside an array of storage locations. If you have a collection of records, each with a key such as a name or an account number, a hash function maps that key to an integer in a fixed range. That integer selects one of the array’s slots, usually called buckets. The hash function is deterministic: the same key must produce the same result whenever the table is in the same shape, because otherwise a lookup could not find what was stored earlier. A useful hash function is also quick to compute and spreads typical keys fairly evenly across the available buckets. It need not be cryptographic or complicated; its job is to make bucket choices look varied for realistic input.

The buckets are the actual working surface of the table. Each bucket is a place where one or more entries can live. An entry normally stores both the full key and the associated value, because the hash tells us where to look but does not itself prove that two keys are identical. When a key is inserted, the table hashes it, goes to the corresponding bucket, and records the key and value there. When a key is looked up, the table hashes it again, goes to the same bucket, and examines what it finds. If the bucket contains an entry whose stored key exactly matches the key being sought, the table returns that entry’s value. If the bucket is empty, the answer is not present. The interesting part is what happens when two different keys are sent to the same bucket.

That situation is called a collision, and a common way to handle it is chaining. Instead of insisting that each bucket hold only a single entry, the table allows a bucket to hold a small collection, often a linked list or a similar sequence, of entries. If two keys hash to the same bucket, both are stored in that bucket’s chain. A lookup then compares the sought key with each key in the chain until it finds a match or reaches the end. This is still fast when the chains stay short, because the hash has already narrowed the search from the whole collection down to one small group.

A small invented example makes the movement clearer. Imagine a tiny table with six buckets numbered zero through five, and suppose a deliberately made-up hash assignment sends the key cedar to bucket two, maple also to bucket two, and pine to bucket five. These assignments are only illustrative; they are not a real hash function and should not be used to infer how any actual hash behaves. Suppose cedar is stored with the value evergreen, maple with broadleaf, and pine with conifer. Cedar goes into bucket two. Maple also goes into bucket two, so it is added to the chain there after cedar. Pine goes into bucket five by itself. To look up maple, the table recomputes the made-up hash, arrives at bucket two, and walks the chain. It compares cedar with maple, sees they differ, then compares maple with maple and finds the value broadleaf. To look up pine, it goes directly to bucket five and finds conifer immediately. If someone looks up ash and the made-up hash sends it to bucket two, the table checks cedar and maple, finds neither match, and reports that ash is absent.

The load factor measures how crowded the table is. It is the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets. A load factor near one means, on average, each bucket has roughly one entry; a much smaller load factor means many buckets are empty; a much larger one means chains tend to grow. When the load factor crosses a chosen threshold, the table resizes. It allocates a larger bucket array and rehashes every stored key into the new array, because the hash’s output range or the mapping to buckets now needs to account for the new size. Rehashing all existing entries costs time proportional to their number, so a single resize can be expensive. Spread over many insertions, however, resizing is usually affordable, and the payoff is that chains stay short and lookups remain quick.

This is where the familiar claim of constant-time lookup comes from. Under a good hash function and typical, non-adversarial keys, the entries are spread across buckets so the average chain length is governed by the load factor, not by the total number of entries. A lookup hashes the key in constant time, goes to one bucket, and compares only a short chain. If the load factor is kept within a fixed bound through resizing, the expected number of comparisons does not grow with the size of the table, so the lookup is expected constant time. That expectation depends on the hash behaving well for the keys actually used. In the worst case, though, every key could land in the same bucket. Then the table degenerates into one long chain, and a lookup may have to compare against every entry, which is linear time. The distinction is not a technicality: it is the difference between a design that usually works like a direct address and one that, for unlucky or deliberately chosen keys, behaves like an ordinary list scan.

That is how the lookup finds its way.
